newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor ahead in Liberian poll, rival protests.
newsitem.headline: Taylor ahead in Liberian poll, rival protests.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor took an early lead in Liberia's elections, edging closer to power in the country he plunged into civil war seven years ago.

But as Taylor's fanatical supporters cheered preliminary results giving him a 62 percent lead, his closest rival Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, polling well below expectations with 18 percent, raised charges of poll malpractice.
Johnson-Sirleaf's allegations of fraud, aired on radio by her campaign manager Dusty Wolokolie on Sunday, were the first sour note in elections praised by monitors as clean.
Wolokolie accused officials of the Independent Elections Commission (IENEC) and troops of the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG of interfering with voting at some stations.
"We've heard of widespread fraud on the part of IENEC officials as well as ECOMOG personnel...We have film to show evidence of ECOMOG casting ballots for people," Wolokolie said.
He was interviewed live on radio from inside the commission headquarters just before elections chief Henry Andrews was to broadcast the first preliminary results.
ECOMOG soldiers, reacting to the interview, halted the broadcast, forcing Andrews to briefly suspend his statement.
ECOMOG commander General Victor Malu confirmed the action of the soldiers but said they had acted beyond their orders.
"They were only told to bring the man (Wolokolie) to substantiate his allegations," Malu told Reuters.

The preliminary official results for about 10 percent of total ballots showed Taylor polling 49,539 votes of 79,403 counted. Johnson-Sirleaf only managed 14,379 votes. No other candidate polled more than six percent.
Taylor supporters, chanting "Taylor has won" poured into the streets of the capital Monrovia, darkened by the country's long-term electricity blackout, after hearing the partial results.
International election experts helping with organisation estimated voter turnout on Saturday at around 85 percent.
A total of just over 700,000 people registered to vote.
Despite being blamed for launching Liberia's devastating civil war in 1989, Taylor is seen by many as the forceful leader needed in the post-war period.
He had overwhelming superior resources to his election rivals, including a national radio station, and ran a well-oiled campaign machine.
Johnson-Sirleaf entered the race late but built up support through her image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Two other former warlords, Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, also ran.
International monitors and Liberia's West African neighbours, who finally rallied the warlords around a peace deal, praised the smooth conduct of the poll.
"The process was smooth, hitch-free and devoid of rancour," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told a news conference on behalf of the West African committee on Liberia.
Ikimi said he and foreign ministers of Ivory Coast, Guinea and Ghana observed voting in Monrovia and in the interior.
More than 500 international observers, including former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, were in Liberia.
